Interviewer: Hi Lena, thanks for joining. I'm Sam, an engineer on the platform team. This is a thirty minute behavioral conversation.
Candidate: Hi Sam, thanks for having me. I'm looking forward to it.
Interviewer: How has your final semester been so far?
Candidate: Busy but good. I'm finishing my capstone and teaching assistant work for the databases course.
Interviewer: Great. I'll ask about three or four past experiences, then leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer [q1]: Tell me about a project you owned from start to finish.
Candidate [q1]: During my internship at Fernhill Payments I owned a tool that flagged duplicate refund requests. Support agents were catching duplicates by hand, about 40 a week. I wrote the design doc, got feedback from two senior engineers, built the matching job in Python, and added a review screen. I chose a simple rule on amount, card and a 48 hour window instead of a model, because we had no labeled data. After launch it caught 92 percent of duplicates in the first month and saved the support team about 6 hours a week.
Interviewer [q1]: What would you change if you built it again?
Candidate [q1]: I would talk to the agents earlier. I only met them in week three, and they told me partial refunds also counted as duplicates. That cost me a week of rework. Now I set up a user conversation in the first few days of any project.
Interviewer [q2]: Tell me about a time you worked closely with someone who had a different working style.
Candidate [q2]: In my capstone, my partner liked to plan everything up front and I like to prototype. Early on we argued about whether to write the full API spec first. I suggested we each try our way for one day on separate endpoints and compare. His spec caught two naming problems my prototype missed, and my prototype found a slow query his spec did not. We agreed on a short spec plus a spike for anything risky, and we shipped all six milestones on time.
Interviewer [q3]: Tell me about something that did not go to plan and what you learned.
Candidate [q3]: As a teaching assistant I wrote an autograder for a SQL assignment. I tested it only on my own solutions, and on the due date it failed 30 students whose queries were correct but ordered rows differently. I owned it in the course forum the same night, regraded everything by hand with one other assistant, and fixed the grader to compare sorted results. Since then I collect three or four real student answers before I trust any grader.
Interviewer: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?
Candidate: How do new graduates get their first project on your team?
Interviewer: Each new engineer gets a small, real project with a mentor in the first month, usually something that ships in four to six weeks.
Interviewer: That's all the time we have. Thanks Lena, the recruiter will follow up within a week.
Candidate: Thank you, Sam. This was a good conversation.
"}]}

Transcript:
Interviewer: Hi Tomas, thanks for joining. I'm Hannah, a group product manager here. This is a forty-five minute behavioral conversation.
Candidate: Hi Hannah, thanks for making the time.
Interviewer: How has your week been?
Candidate: Good. We just closed a planning cycle, so it's a relief to have a quieter few days.
Interviewer: I'll ask about four past experiences and probe where I'm curious. We'll keep time at the end for your questions.
Interviewer [q1]: Tell me about a product you owned and a decision you would defend.
Candidate [q1]: I owned the driver check-in flow at Brightwell Logistics for about two years. Drivers waited an average of 22 minutes at warehouse gates, so I led a redesign to a QR code check-in. I ran twelve driver interviews, wrote the spec, and decided to ship to three pilot sites first, even though sales wanted all forty at once. Gate wait dropped to 9 minutes in the pilot, and we rolled out to every site the next quarter.
Interviewer [q1]: Why pilot first instead of launching everywhere?
Candidate [q1]: Two reasons. A bad check-in blocks trucks, so a bug was expensive, and I had no data on gates with poor mobile signal. The pilot showed that at two sites about 15 percent of drivers could not scan. I added a fallback code, which cost the engineers one extra week. That week was worth it. The full launch had a 98 percent success rate with scan or fallback.
Interviewer [q2]: Tell me about a disagreement with engineering or design over scope.
Candidate [q2]: On that project, the lead engineer wanted to cut offline mode to hit the date. I thought offline was the core need because gates often have weak signal. I did not argue opinions. I pulled gate logs showing 31 percent of check-ins happened on weak signal, and I offered to cut the admin dashboard instead. He agreed, because the dashboard could use existing reports. We shipped on the original date with offline mode, and the dashboard followed six weeks later.
Interviewer [q3]: Tell me about a launch that missed its goal.
Candidate [q3]: I launched text reminders for delivery appointments with a goal of cutting missed appointments by 20 percent. After six weeks the drop was only 4 percent. I had assumed drivers forgot, but I had not checked. I owned the miss in our review and then called 15 drivers. Most missed because of traffic or gate delays, not forgetting.
Interviewer [q3]: What did you change after that?
Candidate [q3]: I changed the reminder to include a live arrival estimate and an easy reschedule link. I also set a rule for my team: no launch goal without five customer calls first. The next version cut missed appointments by 17 percent in two months, and the rule is now in our planning template.
Interviewer [q4]: Tell me about a time you explained a hard trade-off to executives.
Candidate [q4]: Last year the CFO asked me to cut the roadmap by a third. I built a one page view with each item's cost, expected revenue and risk, and I proposed dropping three low-return items to protect the gate project. I told them plainly that this delayed two sales requests by a quarter. I also walked the sales head through the reasons before the meeting, so she was not surprised. The CFO approved it in one meeting, and we kept 90 percent of the planned revenue impact.
Interviewer: Thanks, that's helpful. What questions do you have for me?
Candidate: How does your team decide what to say no to each quarter?
Interviewer: We rank by expected impact and cost, then review with engineering leads, and about a third of requests are declined with a written reason.
Interviewer: That's our time. Thanks Tomas, the recruiter will follow up within a week.
Candidate: Thank you, Hannah. I enjoyed it.
"}]}

Interviewer: Hello Imani, thank you for joining. I'm Julian, a director of program management. This is a forty-five minute behavioral interview, and I will push on your choices.
Candidate: Hello Julian, thank you. I'm glad to be here.
Interviewer: Have you been in program management for a long time?

Interviewer: Good. I'll cover four experiences, then there is time for your questions.
Interviewer [q1]: Tell me about a program you drove across several teams.
Candidate [q1]: I led our payment platform migration across nine teams and about 60 engineers over fourteen months. I built the dependency map, ran a weekly cross-team review, and set a rule that no team could cut over without a tested rollback. I was accountable for the schedule and the risk log. We moved all traffic with zero customer-facing outages and finished two weeks early. I handed the weekly review to a senior engineer in month ten, so the program did not depend on me.
Interviewer [q1]: How did you decide the order in which teams moved?
Candidate [q1]: I ranked teams by the risk of the service and how ready the team was. I moved low-risk, ready teams first so we could learn on small traffic. Billing, the riskiest, went last. Two teams wanted to go early for prestige, and I said no, using data from the first three cutovers: a rollback took 40 minutes the first time and 8 minutes by the third.
Interviewer [q2]: Tell me about a time two teams disagreed on priorities and you had to resolve it.
Candidate [q2]: The fraud team and the checkout team both needed the same three engineers from the shared platform group in the same quarter. Each had a good case, and I did not pick a side. I asked each lead for the value at stake. Fraud's number was 2.1 million dollars in avoided losses against 1.4 million in checkout revenue. I split the work so checkout got one engineer plus a contractor. Both leads signed the plan, and both hit their dates.
Interviewer [q2]: Why not just escalate to your director and let her decide? That is simpler.
Candidate [q2]: I considered it. Escalation is fast, but both leads would have lost trust in each other and in me, and I would have needed to ask her again next quarter. I told my sponsor as soon as I saw it, with a recovery plan, and cut scope to the three reports customers used most. We landed with 80 percent of scope and kept the key customer. Since then I check dependencies on every estimate, and I put a security review into every plan at the start.
Interviewer [q3]: Suppose your sponsor is out for two weeks and two teams refuse to move on a shared deadline. What do you do?
Candidate [q3]: First I would find out why they refuse, because it is usually a real constraint. Then I would put the deadline and each team's cost on one page and bring it to their two managers instead of waiting for the sponsor. Candidate [q6]: I introduced a one page launch readiness checklist. I tested it with two teams first and cut it from 30 items to 12 after they said it was too long. Interviewer: Hi Anika, I'm Marcus, a group product manager. This is a forty five minute product case interview, spoken only.
Candidate: Hi Marcus, thanks for having me. I'm ready.
Interviewer: Are you joining from home today?
Candidate: Yes, from home. It is a quiet week, so that helps.
Interviewer: Good. I will give you three or four cases. Ask clarifying questions whenever you like, and I will leave time at the end for yours.
Interviewer [q1]: RideLoop is a city bike-share. Over three months, weekday rides fell 15 percent while weekend rides held steady. How would you approach this?
Candidate [q1]: First I want to clarify the goal. Is it ridership, revenue, or pass renewals? I will assume ridership, since revenue follows. Then I would split the drop into three buckets: fewer riders, fewer rides per rider, and fewer bikes available. Weekday only points to commuters, so my first hypotheses are a new competitor on commuter routes, bikes missing at rush hour, or a price change. I would check bike availability at the top ten stations by hour first, because it is the fastest to confirm and to fix.
Interviewer [q1]: Suppose availability looks fine. What next?
Candidate [q1]: Then I would look at the rider side. I would compare pass holders against casual riders. If pass holders are leaving, I would read exit survey notes and check whether a new bus lane or competitor opened near them. If casual riders dropped, it is more likely weather or pricing. Each answer leads to a different fix, so I would not build anything until the split is clear. I would ask for three days of analysis, then decide.
Interviewer [q2]: Estimate how many bikes RideLoop needs for a city of 800,000 people.
Candidate [q2]: I will work from peak demand. Assume 3 percent of 800,000 people ride on a weekday, so 24,000 riders. Each rides twice, so 48,000 trips. Say 40 percent fall in two commute peaks, about 19,000 trips. A bike does about 1.5 trips per peak, so I need roughly 13,000 bikes. As a cross-check, comparable cities run about 10 bikes per 1,000 people, which gives 8,000. I would start near 8,000 and grow with data.
Interviewer [q3]: You have a small team and three options: add docks in the suburbs, launch a monthly pass, or improve bike rebalancing. What do you recommend?
Candidate [q3]: I would score the options on weekday impact, cost and time to learn. Rebalancing attacks the availability problem directly and needs mostly software and routing, about six weeks. The pass raises retention but only for people who already ride. Suburban docks are slow and expensive. So I recommend rebalancing first, with a target of 95 percent of top stations having a bike at 8 a.m. The pass is second, tested in one district. I would pause the docks.
Interviewer [q3]: Why not launch the pass first? It is cheaper.
Candidate [q3]: It is cheaper, and I would run it as a small test alongside. But if bikes are missing at rush hour, a pass buys loyalty to an unreliable service and could raise complaints. The risk is that we lock in unhappy members. If the data says availability is fine, I would flip the order and lead with the pass.
Interviewer [q4]: Last one. Leadership wants to add e-bikes. How do you decide?
Candidate [q4]: I would ask what problem e-bikes solve. If it is longer commutes and hills, they could expand our reach. The trade-off is cost: an e-bike costs about three times more and needs charging. I would pilot 500 e-bikes in the two hilliest districts for eight weeks, compare rides per bike and revenue per ride, and expand only if revenue per bike beats standard bikes by at least two times. My recommendation is a limited pilot, not a full rollout.

Interviewer: Hi Rohan, I'm Hana, a director of data science. This is a forty five minute case interview, spoken only. Expect follow-up questions.
Candidate: Hi Hana, thank you. I am ready.
Interviewer: How is your week going?
Candidate: Busy, but in a good way. We just closed a quarter, so this is a change of pace.
Interviewer: I will give you three or four cases. They are open on purpose. State your assumptions, and I will challenge some of them.
Interviewer [q1]: Tunelane's new recommendation model raised click-through by 4 percent, but paid conversion is flat. What do you do?
Candidate [q1]: I would first ask what we want conversion to do, because click-through is a means. My hypothesis is that the model optimizes for clicks on familiar music, which does not change a free user's decision to pay. I would segment free users who hit skip limits against casual listeners. Then I would check whether the extra clicks are new artists or repeats. If they are repeats, the lift is shallow. I would run a two week test with paid conversion as the primary metric and thirty day retention as a guardrail.
Interviewer [q1]: Why not just ship the model? Click-through is up.
Candidate [q1]: Click-through is up, so shipping is tempting. The risk is that we pay for more compute and teach the model to chase clicks, which can hurt retention later. I would ship to 10 percent of free users while we learn, since that costs little and keeps the option open. If the test shows no conversion lift, I would retrain with a reward tied to saves and full listens instead of clicks.
Interviewer [q2]: Estimate the daily cost to generate personalised playlists for 20 million active users.
Candidate [q2]: I would estimate per user and multiply. Assume 20 million users, and one refresh a day. Say 2,000 candidates scored per user, so 40 billion scores a day. At about 20,000 scores per second per GPU, that is 2 million GPU seconds, roughly 550 GPU hours. At 2 dollars an hour, that is about 1,100 dollars. Add three times for features and storage, so 3,000 to 4,000 dollars a day. Caching for inactive users could cut a third.
Interviewer [q3]: The ads team wants more promoted tracks in recommendations. The ML team wants to protect quality. How do you decide?
Candidate [q3]: I would reframe it as one budget: how many promoted slots can we add before quality losses cost more than the ads earn. I would ask both teams for numbers, ad revenue per promoted slot and the retention drop per extra slot. Then I would propose a cap, say one promoted track in ten, and test two caps. Ad revenue is real today, and retention is revenue next year. My recommendation is a cap of one in ten, with a guardrail that stops the test if skip rate rises by 5 percent.
Interviewer [q3]: New fact. Legal says we cannot use listening data from users under 18, about 12 percent of the user base. Does your plan change?
Candidate [q3]: Yes, in two ways. The model needs a fallback for those users, such as popularity within a genre, and I would check whether quality drops for that group. For the ads cap, I would exclude them from promoted tracks, which may need its own review. I would split test results by age group so we do not mix groups. The plan holds for the other 88 percent, and I would start the fallback now, since it is on the critical path.

Interviewer: Hi Ravi, welcome. I'm Helen, I lead the data science group. We have forty five minutes, and I want to understand your experience and what you want next.
Candidate: Thanks Helen. I've been looking forward to this conversation.
Interviewer: Where are you joining from today?
Candidate: From home in the north of the city. It has been a rainy week, so I'm glad to be inside.
Interviewer: Good. I'll ask about three or four pieces of your work and your reasons for the move, and we will keep time at the end for you.
Interviewer [q1]: Walk me through the most important model or analysis you shipped in the last two years.
Candidate [q1]: Last year I led the churn prediction model for the subscription product at Alder and Finch, a mid size retailer. Before that, retention emails went to everyone. I built a gradient boosted model on 14 months of usage data, and I spent two weeks on the label definition because my first one leaked future data. In a holdout test, targeted emails lifted retention by 3.1 points and cut email volume by 40 percent. I ran the test and presented it to finance.
Interviewer [q1]: How did you decide the model was good enough to ship?
Candidate [q1]: I set the bar before training. The retention team could only contact 10 percent of users, so I needed precision above 35 percent in the top decile. The model reached 41 percent. A logistic regression got 33, so I chose the boosted model despite the harder explanation, and I added feature importance reports so the team could trust it.
Interviewer [q2]: Tell me about a time you had to choose between a better model and faster delivery.
Candidate [q2]: On a demand forecasting project, a deep model beat our baseline by 6 percent in error, but it needed a new serving setup that would take eight weeks. I proposed shipping the simpler model in three weeks and keeping the deep one for later. I showed the planners that the gain was worth about 40 thousand dollars a quarter, which was not enough to wait. We shipped the simple one, and I wrote down what would make us revisit the choice. Two quarters later that threshold was met.
Interviewer [q2]: What if the planners had pushed for the better model?
Candidate [q2]: I would have asked what decision the extra accuracy changes. If they could show it changes an order size, I would have put the deep model first. In this case their own numbers said it did not, so we agreed.
Interviewer [q3]: Why are you looking to move now, and why this role?
Candidate [q3]: I grew our forecasting work from one analyst to a team of four, and I mentored two of them. Now I want to work on problems where the model drives a product decision directly, not only a report. Your posting mentions ranking and personalization, which is the area I have shipped in twice. I also want a larger scope, with two or three projects running at once.
Interviewer [q5]: Tell me about a project that crossed team lines.
Candidate [q5]: Last spring I worked with the platform team, the pricing team and legal on a data retention change. Our features depended on logs that would be deleted after 90 days. I wrote a one page proposal with the cost of each option, and I ran two meetings to agree on a 180 day window for hashed data. It kept 11 of our 14 features running and passed legal review in three weeks.
Interviewer: Thank you. What questions do you have for me?
Candidate: How does the team decide which models go to production, and who owns them after launch?
Interviewer: The model owner decides with a review from one peer and one engineer. The owner stays on call for the model for the first quarter, then it moves to a shared rotation.
Interviewer: That is all the time we have. Thanks Ravi, we will be in touch within a week.
Candidate: Thank you, Helen. I enjoyed it.
"}]}

Interviewer [q1]: What was your part compared to the rest of the team?
Candidate [q1]: I did the flows, the screens and the prototype. The product manager set the goal and one researcher helped me with the interviews, but I wrote the test plan. I also made the handoff files for the engineers.

Interviewer: Each designer is paired with two engineers and sits in their standup. Designers also review the built screens before release.

Interviewer: Hi Joaquin, thanks for joining. I'm Marguerite, director of engineering for the platform group. We have forty five minutes, and I'll push on your answers a bit.

Interviewer: I'll ask about your largest projects and how you lead. I'll leave time at the end for your questions.
Interviewer [q1]: Tell me about the largest cross-team system you led.
Candidate [q1]: At Marrow Commerce I led the move of our order pipeline from a monolith to event streaming across four teams. I wrote the migration plan, chaired a weekly sync with the four tech leads, and took the on-call risk for the cutover. We moved in three phases over seven months with no customer-facing outage. Order latency at the 95th percentile dropped from 2.4 seconds to 600 milliseconds, and incident pages for that pipeline fell by about 70 percent.
Interviewer [q1]: What was the hardest disagreement between the four teams?
Candidate [q1]: The billing team wanted exactly-once delivery, which would have added about three months. I argued for at-least-once with idempotent consumers. I built a small prototype in a week and showed it handled replays with no duplicate charges in 10 thousand test events. Billing agreed, and I wrote the idempotency rules into a shared guide that two other teams reused.
Interviewer [q2]: Tell me about a technical call where you went against the team's first instinct.
Candidate [q2]: Our team wanted to rewrite the search service in a new language to fix slow queries. I profiled it first and found 80 percent of the time was one badly indexed query and a cache that never warmed. I proposed a two week fix instead of a six month rewrite. I owned the fix, and median query time fell from 900 to 210 milliseconds. I did note that the rewrite might still pay off if traffic triples.
Interviewer [q2]: Why not do the rewrite anyway while you had the momentum?
Candidate [q2]: Because a rewrite stops feature work for two quarters, and the team had committed to three launches. The fix gave us most of the benefit at about 5 percent of the cost. I also set an alert at twice the current traffic, so the question comes back with data, not opinion.

Candidate [q2]: Two engineers were disappointed, since they wanted the rewrite. I gave one of them the profiling work as a lead task and let her present the results. That turned a loss into ownership, and she later led the cache redesign.
Interviewer [q4]: How do you grow other engineers?
Candidate [q4]: I mentor three engineers at different levels. Last year I gave a mid-level engineer ownership of a service migration, and I reviewed her design docs weekly, not her code. I stepped back from the doc reviews after two months. She was promoted in the next cycle, and the migration finished two weeks early. For juniors, I pair on the first three tasks and then stop.
Interviewer [q4]: Say a dependency team just told you they will miss their date by six weeks. How do you re-plan?
Candidate [q4]: First I would find out what exactly is late and what we can build against a stub. Then I would split our plan into work that does not need it, which is usually 60 percent or more, and move that forward. I would tell product the new risk date today and offer two options, a smaller launch or a delay, with the cost of each. I would also offer the other team an engineer for a week if that gets them done sooner.
Interviewer: Thank you. What questions do you have for me?
Candidate: What is the biggest technical risk the team faces this year?
Interviewer: Our oldest data store runs near capacity. Moving it without downtime is the main risk, and we want a tech lead to own the plan.
Interviewer: That is all the time we have. Thanks Joaquin, we will be in touch within a week.
Candidate: Thank you, Marguerite. I enjoyed the conversation.

Interviewer: Hi Dara, welcome. I'm Jonas, a backend engineer. This is a thirty minute technical conversation, with spoken questions only and no coding.
Candidate: Hi Jonas, thanks. I'm happy to be here.
Interviewer: What are you working on at school right now?
Candidate: My senior project, a shared grocery list app, and I teach assistant for the data structures course.
Interviewer: Good. I'll ask three or four questions about concepts and trade-offs, and then leave time for yours.
Interviewer [q1]: Explain how a hash map works, and what happens when two keys collide.
Candidate [q1]: A hash map runs the key through a hash function to get an index into an array of buckets. When two keys land in the same bucket, there are two common fixes: chaining, where each bucket holds a small list, and open addressing, where you probe for the next free slot. In my teaching assistant work I built a chained map in Java for a lab and measured it. At a load factor of 0.75, lookups averaged about 1.3 comparisons. At a load of 3.0 it was closer to 3.5, so the table has to resize.
Interviewer [q1]: How does resizing work, and what does it cost?
Candidate [q1]: When the load factor passes a limit, usually 0.75, I allocate an array twice as big and rehash every key, because the index depends on the array size. One resize costs O of n, but doubling keeps the average cost per insert at O of 1, which people call amortized. In my lab, inserting one million keys with doubling took about 180 milliseconds. With a fixed 1000 buckets it took over 40 seconds. The trade-off is memory, since the table can be half empty.
Interviewer [q2]: Say a web page you built loads slowly. How would you find out why?
Candidate [q2]: I would measure before changing anything. First I open the browser network tab and see whether the time goes to the server response, to large files, or to scripts. On my group project, the product page took 4.2 seconds. The waterfall showed one 2.8 megabyte image and a database query that ran 60 times, once per item. I compressed the image to 240 kilobytes and fetched all items with one query. Load time dropped to 1.1 seconds. I measured three times, because one run can mislead you.
Interviewer [q3]: For a small messaging app project, would you choose SQL or NoSQL, and why?
Candidate [q3]: For a small app I would pick SQL, specifically Postgres. Messages have clear relations between users, conversations and messages, and I want joins and transactions. In my senior project I first used a document store and had to copy the user name into every message. When a user changed their name, I had to update thousands of documents. In Postgres it became one row. I would reconsider if writes grew to many thousands of messages a second, since then sharding matters more.
Interviewer [q3]: What would make you switch away from SQL?
Candidate [q3]: Mainly scale and the shape of the data. If one machine could not handle the writes, even with read replicas and partitioning, I would look at a store built to spread data across machines, like a wide column store. I would also switch if messages had no fixed fields. But I would try partitioning by conversation id first, because moving data stores costs weeks, and I have no evidence yet that we need it.
Interviewer: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?
Candidate: What does a new engineer's first month of code review look like on your team?
Interviewer: Every change gets one reviewer in the first month, and a mentor walks through the feedback in a short weekly session.
Interviewer: That's our time. Thanks Dara, the recruiter will contact you within a week.
Candidate: Thank you, Jonas. I enjoyed it.

Interviewer: Hi Nikhil, thanks for joining. I'm Marta, a machine learning engineer. This is a thirty minute technical conversation with spoken questions and no coding.
Candidate: Hi Marta, thank you. Nice to meet you.
Interviewer: What are you finishing this term?
Candidate: A thesis on text classification. I also did a data internship last summer.
Interviewer: Great. I'll ask about four questions on modeling and evaluation, then save time for yours.
Interviewer [q1]: What is overfitting, and how do you detect it?
Candidate [q1]: Overfitting is when the model learns the training data too well, including the noise, so it does badly on new data. You can detect it by comparing training and validation scores. If training is high and validation is low, it is overfitting. Regularization and more data help.
Interviewer [q1]: Can you give me an example from your own work, and how you fixed it?
Candidate [q1]: In my thesis I trained a classifier on about 2000 labeled reviews. Training accuracy was 99 percent but validation was 81 percent. I added dropout and early stopping, and validation went up to 86 percent. I also tried a smaller model, which was about as good.
Interviewer [q2]: How would you pick an evaluation metric for an imbalanced classification problem?
Candidate [q2]: Accuracy is not good there, because the model can predict the majority class every time. So I would use precision, recall and F1 score instead. Or the area under the ROC curve. It depends on the problem.
Interviewer [q2]: What would you choose for fraud detection, and why?
Candidate [q2]: I think recall, because missing a fraud is worse. But precision matters too, because too many false alarms annoy customers. So maybe F1, or I would pick a threshold together with the team.
Interviewer [q3]: Your model's accuracy dropped a week after deployment. What do you check?
Candidate [q3]: First I would check whether the input data changed, like a new data source or missing values. Then I would look at whether the data distribution drifted. I would also check the code for bugs in the pipeline. If needed I would retrain the model on newer data.
Interviewer [q3]: Which of those would you check first, and why?
Candidate [q3]: The pipeline, because bugs are the cheapest to rule out. In my internship a column was renamed upstream and filled with nulls, and our accuracy dropped for two days before we saw it. After that I added a null rate check on each input.
Interviewer [q4]: Last one. Explain the bias variance trade-off to a teammate.
Candidate [q4]: Bias is error from a model that is too simple, so it misses patterns. Variance is error from a model that is too sensitive to the training data. In my thesis a decision tree of depth 3 got 78 percent on both train and test, which is bias. A depth 20 tree got 99 percent on train and 80 on test, which is variance. You tune the depth to balance them.
Interviewer: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?
Candidate: What kind of mentoring do new data scientists get on your team?
Interviewer: Each new hire has a mentor for six months and a weekly one on one. Most start by improving an existing model.
Interviewer: That's our time. Thanks Nikhil, you will hear from the recruiter within a week.
Candidate: Thank you, Marta. This was helpful.

Interviewer: Hi Imran, thanks for joining. I'm Dana, a staff engineer on the infrastructure team. This is a forty five minute technical conversation. Questions are spoken, with no coding, and I will push on your answers.
Candidate: Sounds good, Dana. Thanks for having me.
Interviewer: What does your team own right now?
Candidate: I'm on a payments platform team of six. We own the ledger service and the retry pipeline behind it.
Interviewer: Good. I'll cover debugging, system design and data consistency, then leave time for your questions.
Interviewer [q1]: Walk me through how you would debug a service whose p99 latency doubled after a deploy.
Candidate [q1]: First I confirm it is the deploy: I compare p99 before and after on the dashboard, and roll back if it is clearly tied to the release, because rollback is cheap. Then I split latency by endpoint and by dependency using traces. At my current job, p99 on the ledger service went from 180 to 400 milliseconds after a release. Traces showed a new database call inside a loop, 25 calls per request. I batched it into one query and p99 came back to 190.

Candidate [q1]: Then I use a feature flag to turn off the new code path if one exists. If not, I ship a forward fix and limit risk by sending only 5 percent of requests to it first, watching p99 and error rate for 15 minutes before going wider. I also tell the on call engineer and the team channel, so people stop making unrelated changes while we investigate.
Interviewer [q2]: How do you choose between a message queue and direct synchronous calls between services?
Candidate [q2]: I ask whether the caller needs the answer now. If the user is waiting on the result, a synchronous call is simpler. If the work can finish later, like sending a receipt or updating a report, I use a queue so a slow downstream service cannot slow the caller. So I choose by how much failure I can tolerate in the user path.
Interviewer [q2]: Suppose finance tells you to cut infrastructure cost by forty percent next quarter. Does your answer change?
Candidate [q2]: The details change, not the principle. A managed queue is a running cost, so I would first check how many messages we send, and whether a database table with a worker, an outbox, could carry the low volume flows. For a flow under 50 messages a second, that is probably enough and costs nothing extra. I would keep the real queue only where volume or bursts justify it, and I would show finance the numbers.
Interviewer [q3]: Switching topics. When would you not use the serializable isolation level?
Candidate [q3]: Serializable gives the strongest guarantee, but it costs throughput and can abort transactions that must be retried. I avoid it for hot rows, like a counter or an account balance updated by many requests, because conflicts rise sharply. For those I use a row lock or a single atomic update. I use serializable for rare, complex rules across several rows where a bug costs money, and I accept the retry logic. On our ledger, moving one hot path to row locks cut aborts from about 8 percent to under 1.
Interviewer: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?
Candidate: How does your team decide which latency targets to enforce?
Interviewer: Each service owns a p99 target agreed with its main callers, and we review misses in a monthly meeting.
Interviewer: That's all we have time for. Thanks Imran, the recruiter will follow up within a week.
Candidate: Thank you, Dana. I enjoyed the questions.

But offline metrics only predict online ones loosely. On my team the correlation between offline NDCG gain and online click gain was about 0.6. So a candidate that clears offline checks goes to a one week A/B test on 5 percent of traffic, with guardrails for latency and complaint rate. I treat offline as a filter and online as the decision.
Interviewer [q1]: What do you do when offline and online results disagree?
Candidate [q1]: I treat it as a finding, not noise. Last year a model gained 2 percent offline but lost 1 percent online. I looked at the logs, and our training labels came from clicks on a layout that no longer existed, so position bias had shifted. We added position as a feature in training and used inverse propensity weights, and the next version gained 1.5 percent online. I also wrote that check into the team's review template so others reuse it.
Interviewer [q2]: How do you decide between retraining on a schedule and retraining on drift triggers?
Candidate [q2]: I start with a schedule because it is predictable and easy to audit. We retrain weekly, at about 400 dollars of compute per run. Drift triggers help when the world changes faster than the schedule, like a sales event, but they add false alarms and are harder to debug. So I use a weekly schedule plus a trigger only for severe drift, such as a population stability index above 0.3 on key features. It is simplicity against reaction time, and I let the cost of stale predictions set the balance.
Interviewer [q2]: How did you measure the cost of stale predictions?
Candidate [q2]: We replayed three months of data and delayed each model by one, two and four weeks. Quality dropped 0.4 percent a week on average, but 3 percent in holiday weeks. That showed weekly retraining was enough except during sales, so we added a manual trigger for those events. I wrote the runbook so two other engineers could run it.
Interviewer [q4]: How would you cut serving cost for a large model without losing much quality?

Interviewer: Hi Gareth, thanks for joining. I'm Elise, an engineering manager. This is a thirty minute technical conversation. I ask spoken questions, I will push on answers, and there is no coding.
Candidate: Hi Elise, thanks. Sounds fine.
Interviewer: How long have you been in your current role?
Candidate: Six years in total as an engineer, and the last two as a tech lead for a team of seven.
Interviewer: Good. I'll ask three or four questions about reliability and design, and then leave time for yours.
Interviewer [q1]: A service has intermittent timeouts under load. How do you find the cause?
Candidate [q1]: I would start with the metrics and logs to see when the timeouts happen. Then check CPU, memory and the database connections. Usually it is a slow dependency or a thread pool that is full. I would use tracing to see where the time goes. Then fix the bottleneck.
Interviewer [q1]: Give me a specific time you did this, and what you found.
Candidate [q1]: We had timeouts on an order service every evening. Traces showed requests waiting on the database connection pool, which was set to 10. We raised it to 50 and the timeouts stopped. I led the investigation with two other engineers.
Interviewer [q2]: Monolith or microservices for a team of ten engineers?
Candidate [q2]: Microservices, I think, because they let teams work independently and scale separately. Each service can use the best technology. It is also more resilient because one failure does not take everything down. Most big companies use them.
Interviewer [q2]: Why not the simpler option? A monolith is easier to build and run.
Candidate [q2]: That is true, a monolith is simpler at the start. At my company we split ours when we had twelve engineers, and deploys went from weekly to daily. But it took about three months and we hit new network failures. For ten engineers I would probably start modular and split later.
Interviewer [q2]: Suppose your largest customer needs ninety nine point nine nine percent uptime starting next month. What changes?
Candidate [q2]: We would add redundancy, so several instances in different zones, and a load balancer with health checks. We would set up monitoring and alerts and an on call rotation. And maybe do more testing before releases.
Interviewer [q2]: How much downtime per year does that target allow?
Candidate [q2]: I think about fifty minutes a year. So we could not rely on manual recovery, and every deploy needs to be safe. I guess we would also need to practice failovers and have good alerts.
Interviewer [q3]: How would you make a payment API safe to retry?
Candidate [q3]: With an idempotency key. The client sends a unique key with each request, and the server stores the key with the result. If the same key arrives again, it returns the stored result instead of charging twice. At my company we added this and duplicate charges fell from about 30 a month to zero. We keep keys for 24 hours.
Interviewer: Thanks. What questions do you have for me?
Candidate: How does your team handle on call load for senior engineers?
Interviewer: Senior engineers join a one in six rotation, and a week on call is followed by a week without project meetings.
Interviewer: That's our time. Thanks Gareth, the recruiter will contact you within a week.
Candidate: Thank you, Elise.
"}]}
